prompt: Dealers are short gamma into expiry, so every move gets chased.
options: Option sellers must buy as the market rises and sell as it falls to stay hedged, so moves get bigger
Dealers have run out of money to buy options, so prices should stay calm until expiry
Dealers own a lot of options, so they will sell into rallies and buy into dips, which calms the market down
Traders are rushing to close positions because expiry has been moved to an earlier day
why: Short gamma means the hedge has to chase the price: buy higher, sell lower. When dealers as a group are short gamma, their hedging adds to the move.

prompt: Results are after the bell. Expect the crush tomorrow even if the stock goes nowhere.
options: Option prices should fall after the results as implied vol drops, even if the stock barely moves
The share price should fall sharply at tomorrow's open, whatever the results end up saying
Brokers will cut the margin on the stock after the results, so many traders will be forced to sell
Trading volume in the stock's options will dry up for the rest of the week after the results
why: Implied vol is bid up before an event and falls once the news is out. That fall, the IV crush, hits option prices even when the stock is flat.

prompt: Give me a two-way in 5 lakh Infy. I'm not telling you which side.
options: Quote a buying and a selling price for 5 lakh Infosys shares without knowing the client's side
Buy 5 lakh Infosys shares in two equal halves, one in the morning and one in the afternoon
Show the 5 lakh Infosys order on both NSE and BSE at the same time to find the best price
Swap 5 lakh Infosys shares for the same value of another IT stock at today's official closing prices
why: A two-way price is a bid and an offer together. Clients ask without saying their side so the dealer can't skew the quote against them.

prompt: Somebody's hitting every bid in HDFC Bank. It's down 2% on no news.
options: A seller keeps selling at the prices buyers are showing, pushing the stock down without any news
A buyer keeps paying the sellers' prices, pushing the stock up without any news
The exchange has cancelled every buy order in HDFC Bank because of a technical problem
A buyer keeps placing new buy orders below the market and patiently waiting for the price to come down
why: Hitting the bid means selling at the price buyers are showing. Doing it again and again is an aggressive seller at work.

prompt: A 25 bp cut is fully priced in. The market needs a dovish tone to rally.
options: Prices already assume the cut, so only a softer message than expected would lift the market
The RBI has already cut rates by 25 basis points, so the market is bound to fall back from here
The 25 basis point cut has been added to bond coupons, so bond prices are bound to fall
Traders have bought protection against a rate cut, so the market is safe from any surprise
why: Priced in means the expected news is already in the price. To move the market, the RBI has to surprise, here by sounding readier to cut again.

prompt: Get me flat by 3:15. I don't want to carry anything into the US data.
options: Close every open position before 3:15 so nothing is held overnight into the US data
Keep the positions open but stop trading until 3:15, when the US data comes out
Bring the book's profit and loss back to zero by 3:15 by adding new trades
Move every intraday position into delivery before 3:15 so that it can be held overnight
why: Flat means no position. The trader wants every position closed before the close, so an overnight surprise can't hurt.

prompt: We're axed to sell Tata Steel. Show it to the long-onlys first.
options: We have Tata Steel shares we want to sell, so offer them to long-only funds first
We're cutting our research coverage of Tata Steel, so tell the long-only funds first
We're barred from trading Tata Steel this week, so pass any orders to the long-only desk
We want to buy Tata Steel before the long-only funds do, so keep the order quiet
why: Being axed means having a position you want to move. A sell axe is shown to the clients most likely to buy.

prompt: Any colour on the Bank Nifty selling? Feels like one big seller, not panic.
options: Does anyone know who is selling Bank Nifty and why? It looks like one large seller, not broad panic
Can someone mark the Bank Nifty chart in red? It looks like panic selling across the market
Is the Bank Nifty selling over for the day? It feels like the panic has already passed
Should we add more Bank Nifty shorts now? It feels like one big seller is about to start a real panic
why: Colour is the story behind the flow: who's trading and why. Desks swap it all day to judge whether a move will last.

prompt: Down 30% in three days. I'm not catching that knife until the selling stops.
options: The stock is still collapsing, so buying now is too risky until the fall steadies
The stock is a bargain after a 30% fall, so it should be bought straight away
The trader is short the stock and wants to close the position now, before it bounces
The exchange will halt the stock soon, so it's best to buy before trading stops
why: Catching a falling knife means buying something still in free fall. The speaker wants to see the fall stop first.

prompt: Everyone's long the same defence names. When it unwinds, the exit door is tiny.
options: Too many funds hold the same positions, so if they all sell together, prices could fall hard
Defence stocks are too hard to buy, so few funds have managed to build positions in them
The government may block sales of defence stocks, so holders could be stuck with them
Everyone has already sold the defence stocks, so from here they can only go up
why: A crowded trade is one many investors share. When they all head for the exit at once, the selling feeds on itself.

prompt: Full risk-off this morning: small-caps getting dumped, money running into gold and bonds.
options: Investors are selling risky holdings like small-caps and moving into safer ones like gold and bonds
Investors are buying small-caps this morning because gold and bonds look too expensive
The market opened late this morning because the exchange was running risk checks
Traders have switched off their risk systems for the morning, which is why prices are jumping around
why: Risk-off is a mood where investors cut risky holdings and look for safety.

prompt: Long build-up in PSU banks, OI up 12% with price. The rally's got legs.
options: Traders are opening new long positions in PSU banks, so fresh money is behind the rally
Traders who were short PSU banks are buying back, so the rally may fade soon
Long-term investors are selling their PSU bank shares into the rally
The exchange has raised the position limits on PSU bank futures by 12%
why: Price and open interest rising together point to new longs. A rally on short covering, with OI falling, tends to fade sooner.

prompt: Heavy CE writing at 25,000. That's where the bears are drawing the line.
options: Many traders are selling 25,000 calls, betting the Nifty stays below that level
Many traders are buying 25,000 calls, betting the Nifty rallies above that level
The exchange has capped the Nifty at 25,000 until this week's expiry
Brokers are writing research notes with a Nifty target of 25,000
why: Writing calls means selling them. Sellers of 25,000 calls profit if the Nifty stays below 25,000, so traders read heavy writing there as resistance.

prompt: Work it at 10% of volume and don't print worse than VWAP.
options: Trade about a tenth of market volume and average no worse than the day's volume-weighted price
Fill 10% of the order now and leave the other 90% for the closing auction at whatever price it gets
Buy 10% more than the client asked for whenever the price drops below the day's average
Show 10% of the order on screen and hide the rest until the price beats the day's average
why: Trading at 10% of volume keeps the footprint small. VWAP is the day's volume-weighted average price, a common yardstick for a fair fill.

prompt: Arrival was 1,412, we averaged 1,419 and missed a fifth of the order. IS looks ugly.
options: Measured from the arrival price, we paid more and left part unfilled, so trading cost a lot
We bought below the price when the order arrived, so the order was filled at a good price
The client cancelled a fifth of the order to save on trading costs, which made the fills worse
The broker's commission on the order was too high, so the average price ended up at 1,419
why: Implementation shortfall compares what you got with the price when you decided to trade, including the cost of the part you never filled.

prompt: Backtest Sharpe of 3 on 18 months of data? I'd bet it's overfit.
options: On so short a test, a Sharpe that high usually means the rules were fitted to noise
Making money every month for 18 months proves the strategy has a real edge
The strategy made 3% a month for 18 months, which is too little to be worth running
The test used too many years of data, so the result is out of date and should be rerun
why: A Sharpe of 3 is rare even for the best funds. On a short sample it usually means the rules were fitted to that history.

prompt: Your signal uses today's close to trade at today's close. That's look-ahead.
options: The test trades on information it couldn't have had at the moment it trades
The signal looks too far ahead, so it holds each trade for too long
The test trades too near the close, when trading costs are highest
The signal leaves out every stock that closed lower on the day
why: You only know the closing price after the close, so you can't trade at it on its own signal. Using it is look-ahead bias, and it flatters the backtest.

prompt: The CAGR's fine. It's the 40% hole in 2020 that'll lose you clients.
options: The yearly return is fine, but a 40% fall from the 2020 peak would make investors quit
The fund lost 40% of its clients in 2020, even though its yearly return looks good
The fund's yearly return was cut by 40% after one very bad year in 2020
The fund had to repay 40% of its 2020 profits to clients who chose to leave
why: A deep drawdown tests investors' patience more than the average return does. Many sell near the bottom.

prompt: The MPC held, but the minutes read hawkish. Bonds won't like it.
options: Rates were held, but the committee sounded worried about inflation, so bond prices may fall
The committee cut rates and hinted at more cuts, so bond prices are likely to rise
Rates stayed the same and the committee promised cuts soon, so bonds should rally
The minutes came out late, so bond trading was stopped for the rest of the trading day
why: Hawkish means leaning towards higher rates or keeping them high. That pushes yields up and bond prices down.

prompt: RBI's selling dollars on every spike, so USDINR won't run away today.
options: The RBI keeps selling dollars whenever the dollar jumps, which limits how far the rupee can fall
The central bank keeps buying dollars whenever the rupee strengthens, to stop the rupee rising too far
The central bank has stopped all USDINR trading for the day after the dollar spiked
Banks have been told not to sell rupees for the rest of the day, so the rate is frozen
why: Selling dollars from reserves meets the demand for dollars and slows the rupee's fall.

prompt: Every time we get filled on that bid, the stock drops a rupee. We're being picked off.
options: Our buy orders mostly fill just before the price falls, so better-informed traders are selling to us
Our buy orders are priced too low, so they hardly ever get filled before the price moves away from them
The exchange is filling our buy orders a rupee away from the price we asked for
Our buy orders only fill in the last minutes of the day, when prices tend to drop
why: Adverse selection is trading with someone who knows more. Fills that keep going against you are the sign.

prompt: Huge bids keep appearing three ticks down and vanish whenever the price gets near.
options: Someone may be placing orders they never mean to fill, to make the market look stronger than it is
A big buyer is patiently waiting to buy at a lower price and will get filled when the price gets there
The exchange is testing its systems with dummy orders that can't be traded
Market makers are raising their bids ahead of news, which is why the price keeps rising
why: Large orders pulled just before they can trade are the classic sign of spoofing, which is illegal.

prompt: Roll's expensive this month. The curve's in steep contango.
options: Next month's futures cost well above this month's, so rolling a long position costs more than usual
This month's futures cost well above next month's, so rolling a long position this month earns money
Rolling is cheap this month because the futures trade below the spot price
Futures have stopped trading for the month until every position has been rolled
why: In contango, later futures trade above nearer ones. A long who rolls sells the near month and buys the next, paying that gap.

prompt: VIX at 11, straddles are cheap. I'd rather own options into the Budget.
options: Expected volatility is low, so options are cheap, and buying them before the Budget looks good value
The market has fallen 11% this year, so now is a good time to sell options ahead of the Budget speech
Straddles are cheap because the Budget has been postponed, so there's nothing to trade
Volatility is high at 11, so it's better to sell straddles before the Budget speech
why: A low VIX means options are priced for small moves. If the Budget brings a big move, bought options gain.

prompt: We need to buy right now, and we'll pay the seller's price.
options: Lift the offer.
Hit the bid.
Work it passively.
Join the bid.
why: Lifting the offer means buying at the seller's price. Hitting the bid is the selling side, and working it passively means waiting for sellers to come to you.

prompt: Don't buy it all at once. Trade it in small pieces through the day so the price doesn't jump.
options: Work it through the day.
Lift the whole offer now.
Go all in at the open.
Print it in one block.
why: Working an order means slicing it over time to limit market impact.

prompt: Sell some of the position, but keep most of it.
options: Let's trim it.
Let's unwind it.
Let's go flat.
Let's double up.
why: Trimming cuts part of a position. Unwinding or going flat closes all of it.

prompt: Your order has been fully filled at the price we agreed.
options: You're done.
You're working.
That's indicative.
You're stopped out.
why: "You're done" confirms the trade is complete. An indicative price can't be traded on yet.

prompt: This price is only a guide. I can't trade on it yet.
options: That's indicative, not firm.
That's a firm price, you're done.
That's a two-way.
That's the last print.
why: An indicative price is a guide that can still change. A firm price can be dealt on straight away.

prompt: The market dipped because traders sold to lock in their gains after the rally.
options: Just profit-booking after the run-up.
That's capitulation after the run-up.
Looks like a dead-cat bounce to me.
It's short covering, nothing more.
why: Profit-booking is selling to lock in gains, often after a strong run. Capitulation is panic selling at the end of a fall.

prompt: My trade hit the loss limit I'd set, so it was closed automatically.
options: I got stopped out.
I got squeezed.
I booked profit.
I rolled it over to next month.
why: Stopped out means the stop-loss closed the trade. Getting squeezed is a short forced out by a sharp rally.

prompt: The price is running away from us. Should we keep buying at higher prices to finish the order?
options: Do we chase it?
Do we fade it?
Do we trim it?
Do we hit it?
why: Chasing is buying higher as the price runs away. Fading is trading against the move.

prompt: I think this rally has gone too far, so I want to sell into it.
options: I'd fade this move.
I'd chase this move.
I'd buy the dip here.
I'd cover here.
why: Fading a move is trading against it, here selling into a rally you think is overdone.

prompt: There are plenty of buyers in this stock at today's prices.
options: It's well bid.
It's offered down.
It's thin.
It's crowded.
why: Well bid means strong buying interest. Offered means sellers are the ones pressing.

prompt: Yields rose by a quarter of one percentage point.
options: Yields are up 25 bips.
Yields are up 25%.
Yields are up 2.5 bips.
Yields are up 0.25 bips.
why: A basis point, said "bip", is a hundredth of a percentage point, so a quarter point is 25 bips.

prompt: The stock rose for weeks before the results, then fell on the day even though the results were good.
options: Buy the rumour, sell the news.
Never try to catch a falling knife.
Long and wrong.
Just a dead-cat bounce.
why: When good news is expected, buyers get in early and sell once it arrives, so the price can fall on good results.

prompt: I bought, and the price has gone against me.
options: I'm long and wrong.
I'm flat on it.
I'm axed to buy.
I'm covering my short.
why: Long and wrong means holding a long position that is losing money.

prompt: Investors are happy to buy riskier assets today.
options: It's a risk-on day.
It's a risk-off day.
It's a flight to safety.
Everyone's de-risking.
why: Risk-on is a mood where investors reach for riskier assets. A flight to safety and de-risking are the opposite.

prompt: The jump came from traders who had bet on a fall rushing to buy back.
options: Short covering, not fresh buying.
It's long build-up, real buying.
It's profit-booking by the longs.
It's capitulation by the bulls.
why: Short covering is shorts buying back to close. It lifts the price without new buyers who want to own the stock.

prompt: Close my intraday position before the market shuts.
options: Square it off before the close.
Carry it forward to tomorrow's session.
Roll it over to next month.
Convert it to delivery today.
why: Squaring off closes an intraday position. Carrying forward or converting to delivery keeps it open.

prompt: Your backtest made 22% a year. What's the catch?
options: The max drawdown was 35% in 2020, and it took 14 months to get back to the peak.
There isn't one: it made money in nine years out of ten, so the risk is low.
It only trades large-cap stocks, so it can't really lose much in a bad year.
It beat the Nifty every single year, so the risk must be about the same as the index.
why: A PM asks about the downside next. Giving the drawdown and the recovery time up front shows you know what could lose clients.

prompt: Does it survive costs?
options: At 8 bps a side for costs and impact, the Sharpe drops from 1.6 to 1.1.
Costs are small for this strategy, so I left them out of the test.
We can negotiate lower brokerage with the broker later, so costs won't matter much.
It trades a lot, so the costs should average out over the year.
why: Answer with numbers: the cost you assumed and what's left after it. Leaving costs out is a common reason backtests fail live.

prompt: How do I know this isn't overfit?
options: I fixed the rules on 2012–19. On 2020–25, which they never saw, the Sharpe is 0.9 against 1.2.
I tested 200 versions of the rules, and this one came out clearly the best of them all.
It works on every stock I tried it on, using the same years I built the rules on.
Its Sharpe over the whole test period is 2.5, so there's plenty of room for error.
why: Results on data the rules never saw are the best evidence. Picking the best of 200 versions is the problem, not the answer.

prompt: Your one-day 99% VaR went from 40 to 75 lakh. Why?
options: We sold a Nifty straddle yesterday. It's most of the increase; I can send the breakdown.
VaR is just a model, and markets have been calm lately, so I wouldn't worry about it.
It's still under the 1 crore limit, so the increase doesn't really matter to us.
I'm not sure why it moved. Maybe something in the risk system's data feed changed overnight.
why: Risk wants the source of the change and to see that you own it. Naming the new position and offering the breakdown does both.

prompt: You're at 265% gross against a 250% limit.
options: Understood. I'll cut the weakest pairs to get under 250% by the close and send you the list.
Net is only 10%, so the gross limit shouldn't really apply to a hedged book like this.
I'll be back under the limit on my own once the market moves my way later this week.
Can we raise the limit to 275% just for this week, while the trades have time to work?
why: A limit breach needs a plan with a deadline. A small net doesn't excuse a gross breach: gross measures how much can go wrong at once.

prompt: It's only right 35% of the time. Why would I run that?
options: The average win is 3.2 times the average loss, so expectancy is clearly positive after costs.
Because 35% is well above the average hit rate for strategies of this kind in the Indian market.
We can raise the hit rate by taking profits sooner, so the numbers will improve from here.
Most of the losing trades are small, so they don't really count against the strategy.
why: Hit rate alone says little. The answer is the size of the wins against the losses, which together give expectancy.

prompt: The client wants 15% of the day's volume done by 11 am.
options: That fast, impact will be heavy. Spreading it to the close would be cheaper; shall I ask them?
No problem. The size of the order won't change the price we get, however fast we go.
Then let's put it all through in the first five minutes to get ahead of the market.
Fine. We'll hide it in an iceberg order, so it won't move the price however fast we go.
why: Trading fast means a high participation rate and more impact. A good execution trader states the cost and offers a cheaper schedule.

prompt: The Nifty's moved 1.5% and our book's delta is way off.
options: Let's re-hedge with futures to get delta back near zero, then keep an eye on gamma.
Let's leave it. Delta always comes back by itself if we wait for the market to settle.
Let's buy more options, so the delta gets bigger and we make more if it keeps going.
Let's close every option position right now and start the book again tomorrow.
why: Delta drifts as the market moves when you hold gamma. Re-hedging with futures restores the hedge.

prompt: Why sell options here? Premiums look tiny.
options: They are tiny: IV rank is 12, near the year's low. I'd rather buy options than sell them here.
Selling options always works in the end, because most options expire worthless.
Tiny premiums mean the options are cheap, so there's no real risk in selling them.
Implied volatility doesn't matter much to option sellers; only the direction of the market really does.
why: With IV near its yearly low, sellers collect little for the risk they carry. Agreeing and saying why is the strong answer.

prompt: Your ten positions are all in different stocks. Is that diversified?
options: Not really: they're all banks and NBFCs, correlated around 0.7, so they'd fall together.
Yes. Ten different stocks is always enough to spread the risk properly in a portfolio.
Yes. None of them is in the Nifty, so they won't move with the market when it falls.
It doesn't matter much, as long as each one is a good stock on its own merits.
why: Diversification depends on how holdings move together, not on how many there are.

prompt: What's the IC, and how fast does it decay?
options: Rank IC is 0.04 at one day, 0.02 at five and gone by ten, so we'd rebalance daily.
The IC is 4%, so the strategy should return about 4% a year after costs.
The IC doesn't decay. Once the signal fires, the edge lasts for as long as we hold the stock.
We haven't measured it yet, but the backtest returns look very good.
why: The strong answer gives the number at several horizons and what it means for how often to trade.

prompt: Why are Nifty options so expensive before the Budget?
options: IV is high because traders expect a big move on the day; it usually drops after the speech.
The exchange raises option prices before big events to protect itself from any losses.
Brokers charge more commission on options in Budget week, and that pushes premiums up.
Interest rates always rise just before the Budget, and that makes every option a lot dearer.
why: Option prices rise with expected volatility. Event days carry higher IV, which tends to fall once the news is out.

prompt: Our fills are 6 bps worse than the backtest assumed.
options: Then the cost model's too light. I'll rerun the backtest with 6 bps more slippage.
That's just bad luck this month. It should even out over the rest of the year.
Then we should trade bigger, so the extra cost is spread over more shares.
The backtest is right. The market has been unusual, so the fills are the problem.
why: Live slippage is real data. Feeding it back into the backtest is the honest response.

prompt: The strategy's lost money for four months. Is it broken?
options: That's within its worst backtest stretch of six months, but I'm checking for a regime change.
It's definitely broken. We should switch it off today and stop the losses before they grow any bigger.
Let's double the size, so it makes the losses back faster once it starts to recover.
It can't be broken. The backtest was excellent, so we just need to wait it out patiently.
why: Compare the loss with the strategy's own history, and check for a change in the market, before deciding.

prompt: PCR is 1.4. Is that bullish or bearish?
options: Depends: put writing means traders see support, put buying means hedging. I'll check the OI change.
It's always bullish. Any reading above 1 tells you the market is going to go up from here.
It's always bearish. More puts than calls means traders are expecting a crash soon.
It doesn't matter either way. The put-call ratio is just noise and tells you nothing.
why: PCR on its own can be read both ways. Whether puts are being written or bought decides it.

prompt: Your fund is benchmarked to the Nifty, and you're 6% behind it this year.
options: We run up to 6% tracking error, so this can happen; most of the gap is our bank underweight.
Benchmarks don't really matter to us. We focus on absolute returns, not on the index.
The Nifty just had a lucky year, so the comparison isn't really fair to our fund.
We'll buy more Nifty stocks before December, so we catch up with the index by year-end.
why: Explain the gap against the risk you said you'd take and where it came from. Chasing the index to close the gap is the weak answer.

options: The stock fell 50 basis points, from ₹100 to ₹50.
The repo rate was cut by 25 basis points, from 5.50% to 5.25%.
Spreads widened by 10 bips after the downgrade.
A 1 percentage point move in a yield is 100 basis points.
why: A fall from ₹100 to ₹50 is 50%, or 5,000 basis points. A basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point.

options: Theta works for us: our long straddle gains a little every quiet day.
Theta is costing us ₹40,000 a day on these long options.
We're short options, so theta pays us while the market stays calm.
Theta speeds up for at-the-money options as expiry gets closer.
why: Time decay works against option buyers. A long straddle loses value on every quiet day.

options: Short covering is pushing the stock down as traders bet on a fall.
The rally is mostly short covering: OI fell as the price rose.
Expect short covering if the results beat; lots of traders are short.
Once the short covering stopped, the stock drifted back down.
why: Short covering is buying back a short, which pushes prices up, not down.

options: It's very liquid: a few hundred shares trade a day, with a wide spread.
Nifty futures have so much liquidity you can trade crores easily.
Liquidity dries up in the last minutes before a long weekend.
We avoid small-caps with poor liquidity; impact cost eats the edge.
why: Low volume and a wide spread are signs of an illiquid stock.

options: We hedged our long Nifty futures by buying more Nifty futures.
We hedged the portfolio by buying Nifty puts before the Budget.
The exporter hedges by selling the dollars it expects forward.
The hedge cost us 1% but saved us 6% in the fall.
why: A hedge offsets risk. Buying more of the same position adds risk instead.

options: Our put has a delta of +0.4, so it gains when the stock rises.
An at-the-money call has a delta of about 0.5.
We sold futures to bring the book's delta back to zero.
A deep in-the-money call has a delta close to 1.
why: A long put has a negative delta: it gains when the stock falls.

options: Implied vol is how much the stock actually moved over the past month.
Implied vol jumped before the results, so options got pricier.
We sell options when implied vol is well above what we expect the stock to realise.
Implied vol usually falls once the event is out of the way.
why: Implied vol is backed out of option prices and looks forward. How much the stock actually moved is realised volatility.

options: Doubling the leverage doubled our Sharpe ratio.
Its Sharpe is 1.1 after costs, which is solid for long-only.
The Sharpe fell once we added a realistic slippage cost.
A backtest Sharpe of 3 usually means something is wrong.
why: Leverage scales return and volatility by the same amount, so the Sharpe stays about the same.

options: Open interest tells you how many contracts traded today.
Open interest at the 25,000 call has doubled this week.
Falling open interest with a rising price points to short covering.
Open interest drops sharply on expiry day as positions close.
why: Contracts traded today is volume. Open interest counts contracts still open.

options: I used a limit order so I'd be filled at once at any price.
Put in a limit order at ₹410 so we don't pay more than that.
My limit order to buy at ₹98 hasn't filled; the stock is at ₹101.
Limit orders rest in the order book until filled or cancelled.
why: Filling at once at any price is what a market order does. A limit order sets the worst price you'll accept.

options: A stock with a beta of 1.5 earns 1.5 times the market's return every year.
With a beta of 1.5, the stock tends to move about 1.5% when the Nifty moves 1%.
Low-beta stocks tend to fall less than the market in a sell-off.
We sold Nifty futures to cut the portfolio's beta before the results.
why: Beta measures how much a stock tends to move with the market, not how much it earns.

options: The governor sounded dovish, warning that rates may have to rise further.
A dovish policy statement lifted bond prices across the curve.
The market read the minutes as dovish and priced in another cut.
Two members sounded dovish and voted for a cut.
why: Dovish means leaning towards lower rates. Warning of hikes is hawkish.

options: My stop-loss got me out at exactly ₹480, even though the stock opened at ₹450.
My stop-loss at ₹480 was triggered when the stock slid this afternoon.
Keep a stop-loss on every intraday trade, and never move it further away from the price.
The stock gapped down below my stop-loss, so I got a much worse fill.
why: A stop-loss triggers an order once the price reaches it. After a gap down, the fill can be far worse than the stop price.

options: VWAP is the average of the day's high and low prices.
We bought the whole order 2 bps better than VWAP.
VWAP gives more weight to prices where more shares traded.
The client benchmarks our fills against the day's VWAP.
why: VWAP weights each trade's price by its volume. The midpoint of the high and low ignores volume altogether.

options: Our longs and shorts are equal, so our gross exposure is zero.
Long ₹60 crore and short ₹40 crore on ₹50 crore of capital is 200% gross.
Risk asked us to cut gross because the pairs are getting crowded.
Adding ₹10 crore to both longs and shorts raises gross but leaves net the same.
why: Equal longs and shorts make net exposure zero. Gross adds them together, so it's as large as it gets.

options: We rolled our futures by closing them and taking delivery of the shares.
We rolled the Nifty longs to next month two days before expiry.
Rollover is high this month, so most traders are keeping their positions open.
The roll cost us about half a percent in carry this month.
why: Rolling closes the expiring contract and opens the same position in the next one. Taking delivery ends the position instead.
